title: Genetic prompt crossover
description: Treat prompts as genomes: keep a population of prompt variants, score each on a dev set, and breed the winners — crossover splices high-scoring prompts' instructions together, mutation tweaks wording. Over generations, prompts evolve toward higher task scores without human rewriting.
method: Population of N prompts; fitness = dev-set score; select top-k; crossover instruction blocks; mutate phrasing; repeat for G generations; keep the champion.
usage: Start from diverse seeds (not N copies of one prompt); keep an elite archive; validate the champion on a held-out set.

demo.code:
import random
random.seed(2)
pop = ['Be concise.', 'Explain step by step.', 'Answer directly.']
scores = {'Be concise.': 0.7, 'Explain step by step.': 0.85, 'Answer directly.': 0.6}
champ = max(pop, key=scores.get)
print('generation 1 champion:', repr(champ), scores[champ])
print('crossover champion x mutant -> generation 2')

title: Bandit-based prompt selection
description: When several prompt candidates compete in production, multi-armed bandits (UCB, Thompson sampling) allocate traffic to learn which is best while exploiting the current leader. The system continuously tests and converges — prompt selection as an online learning problem.
method: Each prompt is an arm; pull = serve with that prompt; reward = task success; UCB/Thompson sampling balances exploration and exploitation.
usage: Define the reward cleanly; start with uniform exploration; let the bandit shift traffic as evidence accumulates.

title: Instruction induction from examples
description: Instead of hand-writing instructions, instruction induction shows the model input/output pairs and asks it to write the instruction that explains the pattern (Honovich et al.). The induced instruction often outperforms human guesses because it's written in the model's own 'dialect'.
method: Provide few-shot pairs; ask the model to induce the instruction; score candidate instructions on held-out pairs; keep the best.
usage: Use diverse pairs covering edge cases; verify the induced instruction on held-out data.

demo.code:
pairs = [('2,3', '5'), ('10,4', '14')]
print('pairs:', pairs)
print('induced instruction: "Add the two numbers." (score 1.0 on held-out)')

title: Few-shot example selection search
description: Which examples you show matters as much as the instruction. Search over example subsets and orders — greedy forward selection, or evolutionary search — measuring dev-set impact. Often 3 well-chosen examples beat 10 random ones.
method: Candidate pool of examples; search subsets (greedy/evolutionary); score with the fixed instruction; keep the best subset+order.
usage: Build a diverse candidate pool first; search subsets before blaming the instruction.

demo.code:
pool = ['ex1', 'ex2', 'ex3', 'ex4']
print('greedy selection: ex2 (+4%), ex2+ex4 (+7%), ex2+ex4+ex1 (+7.2%) -> keep 3')

title: Adversarial prompt robustness search
description: Evolve prompts against adversarial inputs: the fitness function includes worst-case performance over attack suites (jailbreaks, confusing phrasing, edge cases). Prompts that survive evolution are robust by selection, not by hope.
method: Fitness = weighted mean of clean accuracy and adversarial-suite score; evolve; track robustness separately from accuracy.
usage: Keep the adversarial suite fresh; a prompt robust against last year's attacks may fail this year's.

title: Prompt distillation to smaller models
description: A big model's evolved prompt often doesn't transfer to a small model. Prompt distillation re-runs the optimization loop with the small model as the scorer, finding the phrasing that works best for that specific model — prompts are model-specific, and evolution finds each model's dialect.
method: Take the champion prompt; run evolution with the small model scoring; keep the small-model champion; verify the quality/cost tradeoff.
usage: Never assume transfer; always re-optimize for the deployment model; measure the final tradeoff.

demo.code:
print('big-model champion: "Decompose, solve, summarize." (0.91)')
print('re-optimized for 1B model: "Steps: 1) parts 2) answers 3) final" (0.84)')
print('deployed: 10x cheaper at 0.84 vs 0.91')

title: Fitness with multi-objective scores
description: Real prompts trade off accuracy, cost, latency, and safety. Multi-objective evolution (NSGA-II style) keeps a Pareto front of prompts — no single winner, but the best accuracy-for-cost options — so operators can pick the right tradeoff per use case instead of pretending one prompt fits all.
method: Score each prompt on all objectives; keep non-dominated solutions (Pareto front); select parents from the front; evolve toward a better frontier.
usage: Normalize objectives before comparing; present the frontier with tradeoff labels for human selection.

demo.code:
front = [('pA', 0.9, 0.05), ('pB', 0.85, 0.01)]  # (acc, cost)
print('Pareto front (acc, cost):', front)
print('operator picks pB for cheap tier, pA for quality tier')

title: Prompt mutation operators
description: Effective evolution needs good mutations: paraphrase the instruction, add/remove constraints, swap example order, change tone, add a format specification. A library of mutation operators applied systematically explores the prompt space far better than random word tweaks.
method: Define operators (paraphrase, add-constraint, drop-constraint, reorder-examples, tone-shift, add-format); apply randomly per generation; track which operators produce winners.
usage: Log which mutations win; retire operators that never help; combine winning operators.

demo.code:
ops = ['paraphrase', 'add-constraint', 'tone-shift']
print('mutation:', ops[1], '-> "Answer in under 50 words." gains constraint')
print('operator win rates tracked across generations')
